title: Oil Tanker Explodes After Hitting Naval Mine in Strait of Hormuz as Iran Tightens Grip on Chokepoint
excerpt: The blast on Sunday came as Iran's IRGC intercepted six more vessels and traffic through the world's most critical oil corridor has plunged 70% since the ceasefire collapsed.
body:
• An oil tanker exploded after striking a naval mine in the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday, according to Iran's semi-official Tasnim and Mehr news agencies, after the vessel allegedly deviated from an Iranian-designated route.
  • The IRGC claimed it intercepted six ships and fired warning shots in the preceding 24 hours, adding to four vessels stopped on Saturday.
  • Traffic through the strait has dropped 70% since the US-Iran ceasefire collapsed in early July, with only around 15 ships crossing daily compared to over 130 before the conflict.
  • Brent crude has settled above $100 per barrel, with Goldman Sachs warning it could exceed $120 in Q4 if disruptions persist.

The Blast

An unidentified oil tanker caught fire and exploded in the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday after reportedly striking a naval mine, according to Iran's military-linked Tasnim news agency and the semi-official Mehr News Agency.

https://x.com/AJENews/status/2081353237232263454

Preliminary reports, cited by Iranian state media, said the vessel had deviated from a route designated by Iran and entered a mined area outside the safe maritime traffic corridor. Iran had repeatedly warned commercial ships against using non-approved routes through the strait, threatening consequences for non-compliance.

The identity of the tanker, its flag state, and the fate of its crew have not been confirmed. No immediate official statement from Iranian authorities addressed the circumstances of the blast, though the reporting from IRGC-linked outlets carried an implicit warning to other vessels.

Iran's Escalating Control

The explosion came amid a broader campaign by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps to assert dominance over the strait. The IRGC claimed it intercepted six ships over the preceding 24 hours, forcing them to turn back after attempting what Tehran called an "unauthorized crossing." Warning shots were fired at the vessels. On Saturday, four additional ships were reportedly stopped.

Since the US-Iran ceasefire collapsed in early July, the IRGC has attacked at least 11 ships attempting to cross the Strait of Hormuz, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations. At least 17 mariners have been killed in the strait since the broader conflict began on February 28, the United Nations' International Maritime Organization has reported.

"The strait is under our control and completely closed. No tanker will be allowed to enter or leave without coordination with Iran."

— Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps statement, July 23

Traffic Has Collapsed

The strait, which once saw more than 130 ships pass through daily carrying roughly 20% of the world's oil supply, has become a near-ghost lane. Traffic has fallen approximately 70%, with just 15 ships crossing on some recent days, according to maritime data provider Kpler.

The vast majority of vessels still transiting use Iran's approved northern route or employ shadow-fleet tactics. Only 13 ships have used the US-backed southern Omani route since July 6, and on some days, none have attempted it. The Institute for the Study of War noted that it could not independently verify Iranian claims of mine strikes on the southern route.

The US has encouraged ships to use the southern lane to challenge Iran's control, while Tehran insists all traffic must use its designated corridor near the Iranian coast, where it eventually plans to charge transit fees.

Oil Markets React

The disruption has pushed Brent crude above $100 per barrel. Goldman Sachs warned that if the strait remains disrupted through 2027, Brent could exceed $120 in the fourth quarter and average $100 next year. Analysts estimate the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb strait together carry the equivalent of roughly a quarter of the world's oil supply.

The crisis deepened further when Yemen's Houthis, backed by Iran, attacked two Saudi Arabian oil tankers in the Red Sea last week, threatening to impose a naval blockade on Saudi shipments through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. One of the Saudi tankers was set ablaze, according to the Saudi state news agency SPA. The attacks opened a second front in what has become a stranglehold on the world's energy arteries.

Diplomacy vs. Escalation

President Trump halted US strikes against Iran over the weekend in favor of pushing for diplomacy, though he insisted the US remained "locked and loaded" if Tehran did not comply with demands to open the waterway. Earlier in the week, Trump threatened to "bomb and destroy one bridge or power plant" for every ship Iran attacks.

Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei said talks between Iran and Oman on safe navigation through the strait were "useful and forward-looking," with discussions held at the deputy foreign minister level on July 25-26. However, he maintained there had been no change in the status of maritime traffic.

For energy-importing nations, the stakes are enormous. India, which sources approximately 60% of its crude oil from the Persian Gulf, faces particular exposure. A prolonged closure of the strait would force Indian refiners to seek costlier alternatives at a time when global supply is already strained. With more than 15 million barrels per day at risk across the region's chokepoints, the tanker explosion on Sunday is another reminder that the corridor between diplomacy and full-scale energy crisis is narrowing fast.
nri_angle: India sources roughly 60% of its crude oil from the Persian Gulf, making the Strait of Hormuz disruption a direct threat to fuel prices and energy security for the Indian economy and its diaspora.
